title: Incorruptibles, honestly
hook: some saints' bodies decay less than expected; the Church does not treat this as proof

segments.voice: Yesterday, your local shrine: a grotto off the highway, and Jacob waking on a stone pillow to find the Lord was in that place. Your line was close to home.

A glass case in a side chapel. Inside, a nun lies as if asleep, hands folded, face calm. A sign says she died long ago. Tourists lean in close. One whispers that it's a miracle. Another whispers that it must be wax. A child asks, loudly, whether she's real. Nobody quite knows what to say. Here's what neither whisperer may expect: the Catholic Church doesn't count this as proof of anything. Not of holiness, not of a miracle, not of the faith.
screen: `A NUN IN A GLASS CASE.` → `MIRACLE, OR WAX?` → `THE CHURCH SAYS: NOT PROOF.`

segments.voice: Incorruptibles is the name people give to saints whose bodies, when their tombs were opened, had decayed less than expected. The word sounds like a perfect body; the honest picture is often different. Some are dried, darkened or partly preserved, and some on display have faces and hands covered with wax or a mask, which some shrines say openly when asked. Next, what the Church does with it. Investigating a candidate for sainthood, it looks at a life of heroic virtue and at miracles attributed to the person's prayers after death, such as healings doctors cannot explain. A preserved body isn't on that list. Saints' remains have also decayed in the ordinary way, and that counts against no one. So the Church's posture is careful: interesting, worth studying, not proof. Then, why honor the remains at all. The body matters in Catholic belief. Paul writes of the resurrection of the dead, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is sown in corruption, it shall rise in incorruption." The hope isn't a body that stays fresh in a glass case. It's that God raises the dead, whatever state the tomb is in. A decayed saint and a preserved saint share the same promise. Last, honesty itself. Some cases have natural explanations: dry air, the burial place, embalming. Some are still debated. A Catholic is free to say, calmly, we don't know. Faith that needed a perfect corpse to stand up would be fragile, and the Church doesn't ask anyone to lean on it.
screen: `DECAYED LESS THAN EXPECTED.` · `NOT ON THE CHURCH'S LIST.` · `SOWN IN CORRUPTION.` · `WE DON'T KNOW, SAID CALMLY.` · then, large: `IT SHALL RISE IN INCORRUPTION.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one real open question, about faith or the world, that you can't answer; not a debate you want to win. Notice any pull to settle it fast, obviously yes or obviously no, let the pull pass, and say quietly, I don't know yet. If you pray, offer the question to God as it is, unfinished; if you don't, just let it stay open.
Incorruptibles. Saints whose bodies decayed less than expected. Honored, studied, and never treated by the Church as proof. Today's word.
Your line: not proof. Honored, studied, and held calmly, with nothing leaning on it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics venerate the relics of saints, including some whose bodies are displayed in churches; the Church does not treat a body's preservation as a miracle or as evidence in canonization, which looks at heroic virtue and miracles attributed to the saint's intercession.

pairs: heroic virtue and miracles after death

fork.setup: a saint's tomb is opened and the body is found remarkably preserved. people start calling it proof. what does the Church do?
options: declare it a miracle at once.
study it with interest, and decline to call it proof.
close the tomb and forbid any talk of it.
fork.reveal: the Church treats it as interesting and worth study, and does not count it as proof of holiness or of the faith.

original.note: Greek of 1 Corinthians 15:42: incorruption, what Paul says the dead are raised in.

trapdoor: what you thought: some saints' bodies never decay, and that proves they're saints.
what it means: some bodies decayed less than expected; the Church honors them but does not treat this as proof.
what a scholar hears: canonization rests on heroic virtue and attested miracles; Paul's word aphtharsia, incorruption, names a resurrection hope, not a preserved corpse.
guess: saints whose bodies decayed less than expected

chat.says: If a saint's body doesn't decay, doesn't that prove the Catholic faith is true?
options: The Church doesn't treat it as proof; sainthood looks at heroic virtue and miracles instead.
Yes; a preserved body is the main miracle the Church needs to declare a saint.
Yes; every true saint's body stays whole, so a decayed one wasn't really holy.
chat.meaning: A preserved body isn't on the Church's list for sainthood. It's interesting and worth studying, not proof, and decayed saints share the same promise.

Incorruptibles.meaning: saints whose bodies decayed less than expected

heroic virtue.meaning: goodness lived to a remarkable degree, examined for sainthood

embalming.meaning: treating a body to slow its decay

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an old Catholic English translation of the Bible

notes: Claims needing confirmation: that incorruption is not among the criteria for canonization; that canonization weighs heroic virtue and miracles attributed to intercession; that some displayed bodies have wax coverings or masks (e.g. Bernadette at Nevers, not named) and shrines acknowledge this.
Generalizations softened to 'some' and 'have also decayed'; confirm.
Natural explanations listed (dry air, burial place, embalming) are offered as possibilities, not findings.
The hook's nun in a glass case is a composite scene; no saint named.
Douay-Rheims wording of 1 Corinthians 15:42; Greek ἀφθαρσία and pronunciation: confirm.
